While he argues that corroboration reports only past performance, his insistence that scientists *must* prefer the better-corroborated theory for action implies a normative rule that only makes sense if past performance is a guide to future reliability. This creates a 'crypto-induction' where the logic denies what the methodology requires.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the 'normative rule' is reinterpreted purely as a convention for stopping inquiry temporarily rather than a guide to action.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'action' is limited to 'further testing' rather than 'technological application'.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The inconsistency arises from the dual role of the scientist as both a logician (analyzing the structure of theories) and an agent (acting in the world). As a logician, Popper successfully severs the link between survival and truth. As an agent, he cannot help but rely on the heuristic that 'what worked won't fail immediately,' which is the definition of inductive reasoning. The system holds only by compartmentalizing these roles, a separation that breaks down in actual scientific practice.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
